description: Curated vLLM flags. Catalog structure inspired by vllm-cli (Chen-zexi, MIT).

flags.label: Port
flags.help: The network port the server answers on. Apps connect to http://localhost:PORT/v1. Change it only if another program already uses this port; if the port is taken when you launch, the launcher picks the next free one.

flags.label: Context window size
flags.help: The most text the model can work with at once: your prompt, the conversation so far, and its reply, counted in tokens (a token is about ¾ of a word). A bigger window needs more GPU memory for conversation memory (the KV cache). 8192 covers normal chat; raise it for long documents or large code files.

flags.label: GPU memory usage limit
flags.help: The share of each GPU's memory vLLM claims at startup, for the model plus conversation memory. vLLM takes this whole amount up front, even if it ends up needing less. Higher values leave room for a longer context or more simultaneous requests; too high and the launch fails if your desktop or another program is using the same GPU. 0.85 is a safe starting point on a card that also drives a monitor.

flags.label: Number of GPUs to split across
flags.help: Splits every layer of the model across this many GPUs (tensor parallelism), so a model too big for one card can run, and generation usually gets faster too. The GPUs exchange data on every step, so matched cards on fast connections work best. It can't exceed the number of GPUs you have, and the model has to divide evenly across them; 1, 2, 4 or 8 are the safe choices.

flags.label: Simultaneous requests
flags.help: The most requests vLLM works on at the same time. Each active request holds its own conversation memory, so higher values reserve more GPU memory. If it's just you, 1–4 keeps memory use low and predictable; raise it when several people or batch jobs share the server.

flags.label: Math precision
flags.help: The number format for the model's calculations. 'auto' uses the format the model was published in (usually bfloat16) and suits almost everyone. float16 is for older GPUs without bfloat16 support (NVIDIA cards older than the RTX 30 series); running a bfloat16 model in float16 can occasionally overflow and produce errors or nonsense.

flags.label: Quantization override
flags.help: Forces vLLM to treat the weights as a specific compressed (quantized) format instead of reading the format from the model's files. Normally leave this empty: vLLM detects it, and a wrong value stops the launch with an error. The main exception is 'fp8' on a full-precision model, which compresses it while loading to roughly half the memory, at a small cost in quality; it runs best on RTX 40-series or newer GPUs.

flags.label: Conversation memory compression
flags.help: Stores conversation memory (the KV cache, which holds the model's working notes on everything it has read so far) in 8-bit 'fp8' instead of 16-bit. That roughly halves its size, so a longer context or more simultaneous requests fit, usually with only a small loss in accuracy. A good first thing to try when a model barely fits.

flags.label: Use MTP (multi-token prediction)
flags.help: Some models, such as DeepSeek-V3, GLM-4.5, Qwen3-Next and MiMo, include extra layers that guess the next few tokens ahead. The main model checks those guesses all at once and keeps the ones it agrees with, so text often arrives noticeably faster, with the same quality. The gain is biggest for one user at a time and shrinks when many requests run at once, and the extra layers use a little more GPU memory. The launcher checks your model and installed vLLM, picks the setting that version expects, and tells you if MTP needs a vLLM update.

flags.label: Spill to system RAM (GB per GPU)
flags.help: Keeps this many GB of each GPU's share of the model in system RAM and copies it to the GPU when needed. This lets a model that is slightly too big run at all, but every generated token waits on those copies over the PCIe slot, so expect generation to be many times slower (around 10x). A last resort: a smaller or more compressed version of the model is usually the better choice.

flags.label: Disable CUDA graphs
flags.help: Turns off CUDA graphs, a speed-up where vLLM records the GPU's work once at startup and replays it for every token. Recording takes extra GPU memory and startup time, so turning it off starts faster and saves a little memory, but generation gets noticeably slower. Use it only when a model runs out of memory right at the end of startup, or while troubleshooting.

flags.label: Reuse repeated prompts
flags.help: Keeps the already-processed start of earlier prompts in spare GPU memory and reuses it when a new request begins the same way, such as a long system prompt, a shared document, or an ongoing chat. That text isn't re-read, so replies start sooner. It only uses memory that would otherwise sit idle, so leave it on unless troubleshooting.

flags.label: Smooth long-prompt processing
flags.help: Reads long prompts in slices, taking turns with generating text for other requests, so one long prompt doesn't freeze everyone else's replies. It also limits the temporary memory a long prompt needs. Leave it on; turn it off only when troubleshooting.

flags.label: Tokens processed per step
flags.help: The most tokens vLLM processes in one step, across all requests. Larger values read long prompts faster but need more temporary GPU memory; smaller values keep other users' replies flowing while a long prompt is being read. Leave empty for vLLM's automatic choice.

flags.label: Text-only mode (skip vision/audio)
flags.help: For models that can also see images or hear audio: turn this on if you only need text chat. It skips loading the image and audio parts of the model, which frees GPU memory, often enough to make a model fit that otherwise wouldn't. Leave it off if you want to send images or audio.

flags.label: Allow model's custom code
flags.help: Some models need Python code from their own repository to load. This lets vLLM download that code and run it on your computer with your permissions, just like installing a program from that author. Turn it on only for models from publishers you trust. If a model needs it, the launch fails with an error that mentions trust_remote_code.

flags.label: Thinking-model format
flags.help: For 'thinking' models, which write out step-by-step reasoning before the answer. The parser separates that reasoning from the final reply so apps can show or hide it. Choose the one for your model's family; a mismatched one can stop the launch or mix the reasoning into the answer. Leave empty for ordinary models.

flags.label: Tool-calling format
flags.help: Lets the model use tools (functions an app offers, such as web search or a calculator) in apps that support it. The parser converts the model's tool requests into the standard format apps expect. Pick the one for your model's family; leave empty for plain chat.

flags.label: Model name shown to apps
flags.help: A short, friendly name apps see and send instead of the long repository path. Optional.

flags.label: API key (password)
flags.help: If set, apps must send this key, like a password, to use the server. Recommended when other devices can reach this computer, for example with local network access turned on in Settings.

flags.label: Which GPUs to use
flags.help: Which GPUs vLLM may use, by the numbers nvidia-smi shows (e.g. '0,1' for both, '1' for only the second card). Leaving out the card that drives your monitor keeps its memory free for the desktop and avoids startup failures. Leave empty to use all GPUs.

flags.label: Hugging Face access token
flags.help: Needed only for gated models (such as Llama) that ask you to accept a license on huggingface.co before downloading. Create a token at huggingface.co/settings/tokens.

flags.label: Interleave memory across NUMA nodes
flags.help: On computers with more than one CPU socket (and a few very large single CPUs), each group of cores has its own bank of memory, called a NUMA node, and reaching another node's memory is slower. This spreads vLLM's system-RAM use evenly across all nodes (Linux only; needs the numactl tool). That can steady the speed when a large part of the model sits in system RAM, but it can also be slower than keeping memory next to the cores that use it. It doesn't change which cores do the work. It has no effect on single-node machines, which includes most desktops, and it's worth measuring before keeping.

flags.label: Extra raw flags
flags.help: More vLLM command-line flags, typed exactly as you would in a terminal (e.g. --seed 42). They go at the end of the command, so they override the settings above. The launcher can't check them, so its memory estimate becomes a rough guide only.

flags.label: Linear computation backend
flags.help: Chooses the code that runs the model's main matrix math. Automatic lets vLLM pick the best one for your model and GPU; leave it there unless you are comparing speeds. b12x and flashinfer_b12x are for Blackwell GPUs with compute capability 12.0 or 12.1 (such as the RTX 5060 Ti), and b12x also needs the optional vllm[b12x] package. From vLLM 0.30, compatible NVFP4 models get the fast path automatically, and forcing a backend doesn't guarantee more speed.

flags.label: MoE expert computation backend
flags.help: For mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, which contain many smaller 'expert' networks and use only a few of them for each token. This chooses the code that runs those experts. Automatic is best unless you are comparing speeds. b12x needs the vllm[b12x] package, a GPU with compute capability 12.0 or 12.1, and expert weights in NVFP4 or MXFP4 format, and it can't be combined with expert parallelism (spreading the experts across GPUs).

flags.label: Attention computation backend
flags.help: Chooses the code for attention, the step where each new token looks back over the text so far. Automatic lets vLLM choose; leave it unless you are comparing speeds. B12X needs the vllm[b12x] package, a GPU with compute capability 12.0 or 12.1, bfloat16 math, and conversation memory set to automatic, bfloat16 or fp8. It doesn't work with context parallelism or with latent-attention (MLA) models such as DeepSeek.
